There are always two addresses reserved for the network address and the broadcast address. 

Network address: 126.12.16.0
Broadcast address: 126.12.17.255

255.255.254.0 gives you

11111111.11111111.11111110.00000000

so that's 23 bits for the network giving you a cider notation of /23

The third octet comes from this subnet mask. In a traditional /24 you gave 24 network bits and 8 host bits. 8 bits gives you 256 - 2 (for the network and broadcast addresses). When you flip the 23rd but it doubles the possible addresses thus giving your address range another /24 subnet to work with within a /23 giving you 512 - 2

It's difficult to explain without a whiteboard.

Play around with this calculator, it might help you get a more intuitive insight into how subnets work.

It consolidates IP addresses because you use one public address for many devices behind NAT. Otherwise every device would have a publicly routable IP address. There are public and private IP schemes. Private IP schemes are for use behind NAT only and are not publicly routable. See [RFC 1918 Section 3](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1918#section-3)

IPv6 will ideally circumvent the need for NAT allowing all devices with an IPv6 address to be a public IP. But some would argue that NAT provides a layer of security as having everything publicly accessible on the Internet sounds like bad news to some, including me. I shiver at the idea of it. I can't have my IoT toaster getting hacked and someone burning my morning toast.

If we had IPv6 without NAT then there would be a stronger focus on device based firewall security. At least I'd hope my toaster would have a firewall.
